questions.title: What is the difference between the 'substantial evidence' standard and the 'overwhelming' evidence standard in this opinion?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the standard of review. The court says it reviews the district court’s denial of JMOL of noninfringement under a standard where it reverses only if the evidence points 'so strongly and overwhelmingly' to one side that a reasonable jury could not arrive at any contrary conclusion. However, it says it reviews the jury’s finding of infringement for 'substantial evidence.' Why are there two different standards being applied to the same underlying issue of infringement?

questions.title: How does 'self-contradictory' expert testimony specifically disqualify a jury's verdict under the substantial evidence standard?
questions.question_body: In the analysis of the ’134 patent, the court reversed the jury's verdict because Dr. Wells' testimony was 'confusing and unclear' and 'self-contradictory.' If a jury is allowed to believe a witness (as per the substantial evidence standard), why does the court's finding that the witness was contradictory lead to a reversal? Does the court believe that a jury *could not* have reasonably believed such a witness, or is it a different legal principle?

questions.title: In patent law, when does a claim amendment during prosecution constitute a 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal of prior claim scope?
questions.question_body: Regarding the ’775 patent, the Appellants argued that Finesse surrendered the right to claim products using only 'two signals' when they amended the claim to say 'three signals.' The court disagreed, saying it wasn't a 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal. Can someone explain the test the court uses to determine when an amendment effectively 'gives up' a certain scope of the invention?

questions.title: What is the distinction between 'separately identifiable' and 'unique' signals in the context of patent claim construction?
questions.question_body: For the ’775 patent, the court construed 'three signals' to mean 'separately identifiable' but not necessarily 'unique.' I'm struggling to understand the practical difference in a technical patent claim. If a signal is 'separately identifiable' but not 'unique,' could that mean the same signal is being counted multiple times to meet the 'three signals' requirement? How would that affect the infringement analysis?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate the damages award instead of merely remanding it for a new trial or a different calculation?
questions.question_body: The court reversed the JMOL of noninfringement and then vacated the damages award. Usually, if a court finds there was no infringement, the damages are naturally void. But I'm confused about the procedural step: since the court also reviewed the denial of a 'new trial on damages,' does vacating the award imply that the original calculation was flawed, or is it simply a procedural consequence of the noninfringement finding?
